newsitem.title: USA: American Air passengers scramble as strike nears.
newsitem.headline: American Air passengers scramble as strike nears.

text.p: Jittery passengers of American Airlines scrambled Thursday to save their travel plans for the long Presidents Day weekend as rival carriers looked to take advantage of American's looming pilots strike.
Travel agents said they were swamped with calls from customers nervous about being stranded if pilots shut down American at midnight Friday.
"People are really concerned and upset. They want to be reassured but for some of them, we are not able to give too many reassurances" said Emilie Sugden, an agent at Prestonwood Travel in Dallas.

Others predicted that tens of thousands of American customers will suffer delays in the event of a strike and that many could be stranded. "If it happens, Saturday, Sunday and Monday are going to be disasters," said Abbe Aucoin, a manager at UniGlobe Destiny Travel.

American's management and pilots' union leaders met for a fourth straight day of negotiations in Washington and one union official said they were "not that far apart" on terms for a new labour contract. But the pilots insist they will walk off the job if no deal is reached by midnight Friday.

American, which is owned by Fort Worth, Texas-based AMR Corp., carries 200,000 passengers per day on 2,200 worldwide flights. It has already cancelled 129 international flights scheduled for Friday because it does not want its planes stranded abroad.

Many passengers have booked flights with other airlines but others, especially those who bought cheap advance-purchase tickets, have either double-booked or are hoping American will put them on another carrier at no extra charge.

Rival airlines are delighted at the possibility of picking up American's customers, but dislike double-booking because it could mean large numbers of "no-shows" if American strikes a deal with its pilots and keeps on flying.
"All the airlines are trying to cover their bases and, at the same time, so are the passengers," said Chris Privett of the American Society of Travel Agents.

He said some businesses in the Caribbean, which is widely expected to be hard hit by any strike, were taking drastic action to keep up their peak-season bookings with at least one luxury hotel offering to charter small planes to bring in customers who would otherwise be stranded. Others cut rates for extended stays.

Atlanta-based Delta Air Lines Inc. has taken a hard line by refusing to sell refundable tickets for Saturday, Sunday and Monday on some of the busiest routes where American has a strong presence. They include flights in and out of Dallas/Fort Worth, Chicago, Miami, and Fort Lauderdale.
Even so, Delta spokesman Todd Clay said the airline had "very heavy booking across the system".
Other airlines said traffic levels were already high because of St. Valentine's Day and Presidents Day and that there was little space for refugee passengers on some of the most popular routes.
Most industry experts said passengers who hope to fly to Dallas/Fort Worth, Miami and the Caribbean will face the most problems this weekend.

"We compete with American in the Caribbean but we have limited seat availability already," said Dave Castelveter of USAir Group Inc. in Arlington, Va. "We are near capacity, if not at capacity, for the next few weeks in the Caribbean."
American officials spent much of Thursday negotiating the conditions under which other carriers will accept its passengers.
Most rivals said they have already seen a rise in bookings and some planned to increase capacity on key routes.
Officials at Northwest Airlines Corp. said they might put larger aircraft on routes like Chicago-Detroit, Chicago-Minneapolis and Minneapolis-Dallas where it competes with American.

Carlson Wagonlit Travel, the world's second-largest travel agency, said it will deploy assistance teams at 11 major U.S. airports to help customers find alternative travel arrangements if American shuts down and chaos ensues.
But, while the strike could cause thousands of headaches, some passengers quite liked the idea of being stranded.

"I don't care if i get stuck in San Diego, I'll have that much more time to spend with my fiance," said Lise Mertens, a registered nurse who travelled from Dallas to be with her fiance for the weekend and is scheduled to return Tuesday.
